summaries.example: Imagine a scientist studying how animals behave. If the scientist watches only males, the study may miss important facts about females, mothers, and friendships. A feminist approach asks what was left out and whether old ideas about boys and girls shaped the questions. It can help scientists design fairer and more careful observations.
summaries.summary: Feminist philosophy of biology brings feminist thinking to the study of living things and to the study of biology itself. It asks whether ideas about sex and gender have shaped scientific questions, methods, and explanations. Feminist philosophers have criticized claims that genes, hormones, brains, or evolution alone determine people’s behavior and social positions. They emphasize variation and the many interactions among bodies, development, learning, environments, and social life. They also argue that science is not made by a completely viewless observer: researchers bring backgrounds and assumptions to their work. This does not mean that evidence is unimportant. Instead, careful science may improve when researchers test for bias, include different perspectives, and examine which values guide a research project. The entry discusses these themes through examples from primate studies, sex-difference research, sexual selection, and evolutionary explanations of behavior.
key_ideas: Biology is important, but scientific questions and explanations can be influenced by social values.
Sex and gender are not always simple either-or categories. Bodies and identities show variation.
Feminist philosophers challenge claims that biology proves some people must have certain abilities, jobs, or social roles.
Science can become better when researchers study overlooked groups, question their assumptions, and listen to different viewpoints.
Genes, brains, hormones, learning, surroundings, and social life can work together to shape traits and behavior.
summaries.why_it_matters: Biological ideas can affect how people are treated. In the past, some claims about women’s bodies were used to argue that women should have fewer educational or social opportunities. Studying biology carefully can challenge such claims and make research more accurate. It can also help us notice diversity instead of forcing living things into overly simple boxes.

important_terms.definition: A way of studying biology that uses feminist ideas to notice unfair assumptions, missing information, and the effects of social values on science.
An idea or guess about how living things work that can be checked with evidence.
A belief that one kind of living thing is completely different from another kind, with little variation inside each kind.
The idea that one cause, such as a gene, completely fixes a trait or behavior.
The fact that what we know can be influenced by our history, culture, body, and place in society.

questions_to_think_about: What might a scientist miss by studying only one group of animals or people?
Can a person’s surroundings change how a biological trait appears?
Why is it useful to have scientists with different experiences ask questions?
How can a story or metaphor make a scientific idea seem more certain than it is?

summaries.example: Suppose a study asks why a behavior differs between men and women and explains the difference mainly through brains or hormones. A feminist philosopher of biology would ask several questions: How were “male” and “female” defined? How much do the groups overlap? Were social experiences, learning, and environments considered? Were the data large and varied enough? Could the study’s categories or metaphors have guided what researchers noticed? The point is not to reject biology, but to test whether a simple biological story has been mistaken for a complete explanation.
summaries.summary: Feminist philosophy of biology applies feminist theory and feminist philosophy of science to the life sciences. It investigates not only explicit sexism but also the less visible ways that social hierarchies and gendered assumptions can shape categories, methods, metaphors, research programs, and interpretations. A central target is the tendency to treat sex as a simple binary and to explain behavior through essentialist, reductionist, or deterministic accounts centered on genes, chromosomes, hormones, or brains. The entry instead emphasizes biological diversity, developmental plasticity, environmental interaction, and the possibility of several well-supported explanations for complex phenomena. Feminist philosophers also disagree about how best to understand objectivity. Some emphasize identifying and removing bias; others argue that values are part of scientific reasoning and may sometimes support knowledge. Helen Longino’s social account stresses criticism among researchers with different background assumptions, while Donna Haraway’s idea of situated knowledge stresses that all knowers have partial perspectives. These arguments are applied to primatology, sexual selection, sociobiology, and evolutionary psychology. The overall project is both critical and constructive: it challenges harmful or weak explanations while seeking better biological research.
key_ideas: The boundaries of feminist philosophy of biology are open: it overlaps with philosophy of biology, feminist epistemology, science studies, and biological research.
Its motivations include opposing biological arguments used to support oppression, challenging simplistic dimorphism, and improving the accuracy and ethical quality of biology.
Feminist analyses distinguish removing bias from examining how values can help shape research questions, evidence standards, and explanations.
Situated knowledge rejects a single neutral perspective while still valuing evidence, criticism, and rigorous comparison of perspectives.
Complex biological traits usually have interacting causes. Genetic influence does not by itself establish fixed behavior or a single human nature.

Studies of sexual selection and evolutionary explanations of human behavior require careful attention to definitions, environments, comparison species, cultural variation, and evidence for adaptation.
summaries.why_it_matters: Biological explanations can influence judgments about education, work, family roles, sexuality, ability, and social equality. A claim that behavior is naturally fixed may make social arrangements seem unavoidable, even when the evidence is weak or the behavior depends on changing contexts. Feminist philosophy of biology therefore matters to both science and society: it asks whether research represents biological diversity accurately, whether its categories are well supported, whose interests it serves, and whether different perspectives could expose errors that a uniform research community misses.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical study of biological concepts, explanations, methods, and scientific practice using feminist concerns about power, exclusion, and gendered assumptions.
The view that scientific knowledge is produced by people in particular historical, social, bodily, and material circumstances rather than from a view nowhere.
The position that scientific knowledge is shaped by social values as well as by evidence and formal reasoning.
An assumption that a single factor or small set of internal factors fully explains a complex trait, while other levels of explanation are treated as unimportant.
An explanation that treats a trait or behavior as fixed by biological causes, often leaving little room for development, learning, or social change.
The assumption that members of a category share a fixed underlying nature, such as one unchanging nature of males or females.
A research perspective that treats feminist criticism as a check for sexist or androcentric assumptions in scientific work.
The evolutionary study of social behavior; evolutionary psychology often focuses more specifically on evolved psychological mechanisms proposed to generate behavior.

questions_to_think_about: If scientific communities share the same background assumptions, how could an overlooked alternative explanation arise?
When does a useful biological category become an overly rigid binary?
What evidence would be needed before calling a behavior an adaptation?
How might the choice of an animal species as a model affect the conclusions researchers draw about humans?
Can social values both distort scientific inquiry and help researchers notice important questions?

summaries.example: A class investigates whether a certain behavior is “naturally” more common in boys than girls. A feminist philosophy of biology approach would not immediately blame genes or brains. Students might ask how the behavior was defined, whether the groups overlap, and whether family life, school expectations, culture, and learning were included. They might also ask whether the study looked only at boys’ activities and ignored similar behavior in girls. The goal is to improve the question and the evidence, not to say that biology never matters.
summaries.summary: Feminist philosophy of biology uses feminist ideas to examine biology, its concepts, and the way biological research is carried out. It asks whether scientific accounts of sex, gender, behavior, and evolution have been shaped by stereotypes or by social hierarchies. Feminist philosophers have criticized essentialist, reductionist, and deterministic explanations that treat males and females as two fixed kinds or present genes, hormones, brains, or chromosomes as complete explanations of behavior. They stress that biology includes variation and that traits develop through relationships among genes, bodies, environments, learning, and social conditions. The field includes several approaches. Some researchers focus on finding and removing sexist or androcentric bias. Others argue that values are not merely unwanted distractions: they can influence which questions are asked, what counts as good evidence, and whose interests research serves. The idea of situated knowledge adds that every researcher works from a particular social and material position, so no one automatically sees everything from a perfectly neutral viewpoint. The entry uses primatology, sex-difference research, sexual selection, sociobiology, and evolutionary psychology to show why definitions, methods, evidence, and model organisms matter.
key_ideas: Feminist philosophers study both claims about sex and gender and general ideas about how biology explains life.
They question biological arguments that have been used to support women’s oppression or to make social inequality seem natural.
They emphasize that sex, gender, and gender/sex can involve different features and that human bodies and identities do not fit one simple binary.
A feminist critique may act like a scientific check for hidden sexist or male-centered assumptions, but some philosophers also argue that values can help produce knowledge.
Research is stronger when it considers many perspectives, examines overlooked groups, and explains how genes, bodies, development, environments, and societies interact.
Feminist analyses of animal behavior and evolution challenge simple pictures of active males and passive females and ask whether evolutionary claims are supported by evidence.
summaries.why_it_matters: Science can shape everyday beliefs and public decisions. Biological arguments have sometimes been used to claim that women are naturally less suited for education, leadership, or certain careers. Feminist philosophy of biology examines whether such claims overlook diversity, confuse influence with determination, or reflect the society in which the research was produced. This matters because better questions and broader evidence can lead to more reliable science and reduce the chance that scientific language will reinforce unfair treatment.

important_terms.definition: The study of biology and scientific practice using feminist tools to examine gender assumptions, power, missing evidence, and ways to make explanations more accurate.
A scientific or philosophical claim that a person’s social setting, culture, body, and history can affect what they notice and know.
The idea that science is influenced by values, including choices about which questions matter and whose needs research serves.
Explaining a complicated trait mainly through one level or cause, such as genes, while overlooking development, learning, or surroundings.
The belief that biology fixes a trait or behavior so strongly that change is unlikely or impossible.
The belief that a category has one basic nature shared by all its members, with little meaningful variation.
A two-part classification, such as male/female, treated as complete and natural even when organisms show more variation.
The process by which some inherited differences become more common because they affect reproductive success in a particular environment.

questions_to_think_about: Why might studying only male animals lead to a misleading picture of a species?
What is the difference between saying biology influences a trait and saying biology completely determines it?
How could a researcher’s background affect the questions they ask?
Why should scientists explain exactly what they mean by a behavior such as “aggression” or “choice”?
Can a scientific model be elegant and still rely on assumptions that need testing?
